name: Release automation
summary: Tools that turn merged changes into a release without hand edits: they pick the next version number, write the changelog, tag the commit and publish the package.
howItWorks: Cutting a release is four mechanical steps: choose the next version, record what changed, tag the commit, and publish the artifacts. Release tools do them from information already in the repository. Most follow Semantic Versioning, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where an incompatible API change bumps the major number, a backward-compatible feature the minor, and a backward-compatible fix the patch. Tools differ first in where the bump comes from. semantic-release and release-please read the Conventional Commits since the last version tag: `fix:` means a patch, `feat:` a minor, and a `!` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer a major; commits such as `chore:` release nothing. Changesets instead has each pull request add a small Markdown file whose front matter names the packages and their bump types and whose body becomes the changelog entry, which suits monorepos where one change touches several packages. GoReleaser takes the version from the latest Git tag, and release-it asks for it in a prompt unless run with `--ci`. Tools also differ in when a release happens. semantic-release runs in CI after every successful build on a release branch and publishes at once. release-please and the Changesets GitHub Action keep a release pull request open that collects the pending version bumps and changelog; merging it is the decision to release, after which the tool tags the commit and creates a GitHub release. Changesets then publishes every package whose version is newer than the registry’s, while release-please leaves publishing to a separate job. Publishing from CI needs registry credentials; npm’s trusted publishing replaces long-lived tokens with short-lived OIDC tokens issued to one authorized workflow, and adds provenance automatically.
analogy: A newspaper’s print run. Reporters file stories all day; at press time the edition gets the next issue number and a front-page index of what’s inside, and goes to every newsstand at once. Nobody retypes the issue number by hand, and nothing reaches a stand without being in the index.
useWhen: Libraries, SDKs and CLIs that others pin by version, where a wrong number or a missing changelog entry breaks users
Monorepos whose packages depend on each other and must be bumped and published together (Changesets)
Teams that want a person to choose the moment of release but no person to do the steps (a release pull request)
avoidWhen: Applications deployed continuously that nobody installs by version: a commit SHA or build number already identifies each deploy
Histories without a commit convention: commit-driven tools will skip or misjudge releases; use changeset files or choose versions by hand
Giving every CI job a long-lived publish token: publish from one restricted job, with trusted publishing where the registry supports it
example: A team maintains a TypeScript SDK at version 1.4.2 with release-please. Over two weeks they squash-merge `fix: retry uploads on 503` and `feat: add progress callback to upload`. After each merge release-please updates one open release pull request, now proposing 1.5.0 because a `feat` means a minor release, with both entries added to `CHANGELOG.md` and the version in `package.json` bumped. On Thursday a maintainer reviews and merges it; release-please tags `v1.5.0` and creates the GitHub release, and a second workflow job, triggered by that release, runs `npm publish` with trusted publishing. Nobody typed a version number.

source: # .github/workflows/release.yml: release every green push to main
contents: write   # push the tag, publish the GitHub release
id-token: write   # npm trusted publishing (OIDC), no NPM_TOKEN
fetch-depth: 0   # every commit and tag since the last release
- run: npx semantic-release   # version, notes, tag, publish

diagram.caption: Each merge to main runs the release job, which reads the commit type: a `fix` cuts a patch release, a `feat` a minor one and a breaking change a major one, while `docs` and `chore` commits release nothing. Every release is tagged, gets notes and is published.

sections.title: Five ways to cut a release
sections.intro: The tools agree on Semantic Versioning and differ in where the next version comes from and who decides when to ship.

notes: GitHub can also generate release notes for a release, listing its merged pull requests and contributors with a link to the full changelog, without any tool in the repository.

story: Version numbers used to mean whatever each project wanted. Tom Preston-Werner, a cofounder of GitHub, wrote Semantic Versioning to get out of what it calls “dependency hell”: if the numbers follow fixed rules, a user can tell from MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH alone whether an upgrade might break them. Version 2.0.0 of the specification was marked final in June 2013. Olivier Lacan’s Keep a Changelog, first published in May 2014 and at 1.0.0 in June 2017, made the matching case for release notes: “Changelogs are for humans, not machines,” and a dump of commit messages is “full of noise”.

With rules for both, a machine could do the work. semantic-release, started by Stephan Bönnemann and first published to npm in February 2015, runs in CI after every green build on a release branch, reads Angular-style commit messages, picks the version, writes the notes and publishes, so releases are “unromantic and unsentimental”. In 2019 two tools put a person back in at different points. Changesets, first built for monorepos managed with the Bolt tool, has each contributor write the bump and the changelog line as a file in the pull request, and Google’s release-please collects pending changes in a release pull request that a maintainer merges when ready. Both released 1.0.0 on npm within three days of each other in May 2019.

The weak point left was the publish credential: a long-lived registry token stored in CI. npm’s trusted publishing, built on the OpenSSF trusted publishers standard that PyPI and RubyGems also follow, lets a named CI workflow publish with short-lived OIDC tokens that can’t be extracted or reused, and generates provenance automatically; semantic-release now recommends it as the default path.

choices.choice: Derive the version from commit messages
choices.why: If commits already say `fix` or `feat`, a tool can compute the bump and nobody argues over numbers. semantic-release says this “removes the immediate connection between human emotions and version numbers”.

choices.choice: A release pull request instead of releasing on every merge
choices.why: release-please keeps one pull request up to date as work lands, so a maintainer can review the proposed version and changelog and choose the moment to ship by merging it.

choices.choice: Intent files instead of parsing commits
choices.why: Changesets lets contributors “declare how their changes should be released” while the change is fresh, and in a monorepo it bumps the packages that depend on a changed one; commit messages can stay informal.

A long-lived write token “can be compromised, accidentally exposed in logs, or require manual rotation”. Trusted publishing issues a token per run, valid only for the workflow the package owner authorized.
